title: Zeros At The End Of N Factorial
statement:
Given a whole number n, return how many zero digits sit at the very end of n! (that is 1 × 2 × … × n, with 0! = 1).

n can be as large as a billion, so computing the factorial itself is out of the question. Aim for a running time that grows with the number of digits of n, not with n.

examples.why: 12! = 479001600. The factors 5 and 10 each pair with a 2 to make one trailing zero.
Five multiples of 5 (5, 10, 15, 20, 25), but 25 = 5 × 5 brings a second five. Counting only n / 5 gives 5.
4! = 24. No factor of 5 at all, so no trailing zero.

hints: A trailing zero is a factor of 10, and 10 = 2 × 5. Which of the two prime factors is rarer in 1 × 2 × … × n?
Count the factors of 5. Every multiple of 5 gives one, but every multiple of 25 gives one more, and every multiple of 125 one more again.
The total is n/5 + n/25 + n/125 + … with integer division. Keep dividing n by 5 and adding the quotient until it reaches 0.

explain.intuition:
Each trailing zero is one factor of 10 = 2 × 5. In n! there are far more factors of 2 than of 5 (every second number is even, only every fifth is a multiple of 5), so the count of zeros is exactly the number of fives in the prime factorisation.

Count fives in layers. ⌊n/5⌋ numbers contribute at least one five. Of those, ⌊n/25⌋ contribute a second five, ⌊n/125⌋ a third, and so on. Dividing n by 5 repeatedly walks through those layers, and there are only about log₅ n of them.
steps: While n > 0: replace n with ⌊n / 5⌋ and add the new n to count.
pitfalls: Returning just ⌊n / 5⌋. Powers of 5 such as 25 and 125 carry extra fives; n = 25 needs 6, not 5.
Computing the factorial, even with BigInt. It has millions of digits for large n.
Building the powers 5, 25, 125, … in a fixed-width integer in other languages can overflow. Dividing n instead avoids that.

solutions.title: Count fives in every multiple of 5
solutions.idea: Walk over 5, 10, 15, …, n and count how many times 5 divides each one.

solutions.title: Divide by 5 repeatedly
solutions.idea: n/5 numbers give one five, n/25 give another, n/125 another. Sum the quotients.

followups: How many trailing zeros does n! have when written in base 12 = 2² × 3?
Find the smallest n whose factorial ends in at least k zeros. (Hint: the count only grows with n.)
